reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / Bradley's Neurology in Clinical Practice
clinicalPearls: An atypical parkinsonian syndrome caused by tau protein accumulation, with early postural instability and unexplained backward falls
The hallmark is a vertical supranuclear gaze palsy, especially impaired downgaze, which may be preceded by slowing of vertical saccades
Axial rigidity predominates over limb rigidity and patients often adopt an extended, erect posture unlike the flexed posture of Parkinson disease
Parkinsonism in PSP is typically symmetric, has little tremor, and responds poorly and only transiently to dopaminergic therapy
A characteristic surprised or astonished facial expression results from frontalis overactivity and reduced blinking
Early frontal-type cognitive change, pseudobulbar affect, and dysarthria or dysphagia are common
MRI may show midbrain atrophy producing the hummingbird or penguin sign on midsagittal images
Poor levodopa response, early falls, and early gaze problems help separate it from Parkinson disease
reference.pathophysiology: PSP is a four-repeat tauopathy in which abnormal tau aggregates as neurofibrillary tangles, tufted astrocytes, and coiled bodies in the basal ganglia, subthalamic nucleus, substantia nigra, midbrain tegmentum, and brainstem nuclei controlling eye movements. Degeneration of the midbrain and its ocular motor circuitry produces the supranuclear gaze palsy, while nigral and striatal involvement causes the poorly levodopa-responsive parkinsonism. Damage to brainstem postural and gait pathways underlies the early instability and falls, and frontal-subcortical involvement drives the cognitive and behavioural features.
additionalDifferentials: Normal pressure hydrocephalus and other causes of gait instability
additionalInvestigations: MRI of the brain to assess midbrain atrophy and exclude structural or vascular mimics
Detailed clinical assessment of vertical saccades and gaze range
Trial of dopaminergic therapy to document the typically poor and transient response
Exclusion of reversible causes such as normal pressure hydrocephalus where indicated
redFlags: Recurrent unexplained falls, especially backward, causing injury and needing safety measures
Progressive dysphagia with aspiration risk requiring swallowing assessment
Rapid cognitive or behavioural decline affecting safety and capacity
Features suggesting an alternative treatable diagnosis such as hydrocephalus
reference.prognosis: PSP is relentlessly progressive with no disease-modifying therapy; mobility, communication, and swallowing decline over several years, and death is commonly related to aspiration and its complications.
pitfalls: Misdiagnosing early PSP as Parkinson disease before the gaze palsy is evident
Attributing frequent falls to general frailty rather than the disease
Persisting with high-dose dopaminergic therapy despite a clearly poor response
Overlooking dysphagia and aspiration risk until a pneumonia occurs
Missing the surprised facial appearance and slowed vertical saccades as early clues
